title: China quietly massed over 100 ships around Taiwan and western Pacific, Taiwan says
dek: Taiwanese officials describe an unannounced deployment larger than China's last declared drill, days before Asia's summit week. Beijing calls its carrier group's activity routine.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China deployed more than 100 naval and coast guard vessels across the waters around Taiwan and the western Pacific in early November without announcing an exercise, according to reports citing Taiwanese security officials. The deployment was larger than "Justice Mission 2025", the last drill around Taiwan that Beijing declared publicly, the reports said.

By Friday the number of Chinese vessels in the area had fallen to about 70, Taiwanese officials said, according to reports. In its daily count for the 24 hours to 06:00 local time on Friday (03:30 IST), Taiwan's Defence Ministry reported 30 sorties by Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels and three other official ships around the island, according to reports.

## What Taiwan says

A senior Taiwanese security official described the operation as "silent intimidation" that included simulated attacks on cities, according to reports. Defence Minister Wellington Koo said China was running "area denial" exercises, meant to keep foreign forces out of the waters around Taiwan. National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu said formations from China's Eastern, Northern and Southern theatre commands, along with the aircraft carrier Liaoning's group, were still active east of the Philippines.

## What Beijing says

Chinese officials have described the Liaoning group's movements as routine training, according to reports. China's Defence Ministry did not respond to questions about the wider deployment. On Thursday, President Xi Jinping used a speech marking the anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth to call for "peaceful reunification" with Taiwan, which Beijing claims as its territory and has not ruled out taking by force. Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's claim.

A separate report that a Chinese submarine test-launched a ballistic missile from the Yellow Sea has not been confirmed by any government, and The Declaration is not reporting it as fact.

## Why it matters for India

The deployment comes at the start of a crowded week of Asian diplomacy. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due in Manila from 16 to 18 November for the ASEAN-India and East Asia summits, where the South China Sea is a standing agenda item, and US President Donald Trump is due to meet Mr Xi in Shenzhen on Thursday.

For India, the risks are mostly economic and strategic. A large share of India's trade with East Asia, including electronics components it depends on from China, Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, moves through the South China Sea and the waters near Taiwan. Taiwan is also the world's main maker of advanced semiconductors, on which Indian electronics assembly and its new chip ventures rely. Any blockade-style operation, even a rehearsal, raises shipping insurance costs and supply-chain risk.

India has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan but runs a representative office in Taipei, and its policy is to call for peace and stability in the region without commenting on individual Chinese drills. The Ministry of External Affairs has not commented on the latest deployment.

The episode also adds to tension inside ASEAN. On 10 November Taiwan suspended investment talks with Malaysia after Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Taiwan is part of China, according to reports.

## What to watch

Whether Taiwan's daily counts of Chinese ships and aircraft rise or fall around the Trump-Xi meeting on 19 November, and whether the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea features in the East Asia Summit statement in Manila.
